A.title: Fund care by reforming the Triple Lock, with pensioner floor and audit
A.answer: Keep councils commissioning care, but change the rules. First, the Treasury publishes the Triple Lock change as a costed schedule, with a protected floor so no pensioner's income falls; the poll found 48% support when it funds care (s2). Second, the Department of Health and Social Care makes the neighbourhood-zone guidance (due spring, s1) conditional on carers' fair pay agreement and visit-time minimums, backed by the extra £4.6 billion for councils (s1). Third, an independent auditor reports yearly on visit length, carer travel time and the Bristol-style savings claim of 35% less staff time (s1). It worked if savings reach pay and visit time, and no pensioner loses.

B.title: Let carers and people receiving care co-own each neighbourhood's home care
B.answer: The government wants one or two main home care providers per neighbourhood, and toolkits for councils are due in spring [s1]. Make the toolkit favour providers owned and run by their own carers and the people they visit, so the neighbourhood team, not a distant head office, sets rotas, visit lengths and pay under the planned fair pay agreement [s1]. Councils would award the neighbourhood contracts on that basis. Study: zoned visits could cut staff time 35% and driving 65% [s1]; let the team keep that saving for pay and longer visits. You would know it worked if the same carers keep turning up, visits are not cut short, and carers stay. Simulated citizens backing familiar local faces: 32 of the panel.
